docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Trajectopy - Trajectory Evaluation in Python Trajectopy is a Python package with an optional graphical user interface for empirical trajectory evaluation.

Trajectopy compares an estimated trajectory, e.g. from SLAM, visual odometry or GNSS/INS, with a reference (ground truth). It aligns both in space and time, computes the absolute and relative trajectory error and shows the deviations in plots, reports and Google Earth.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Alignment: a spatio-temporal least squares alignment that estimates a similarity transformation, a time shift and a leverarm, each of them optional, weighted by the accuracies of both trajectories.
  • Evaluation: absolute trajectory error (ATE) with along-track and cross-track components, relative pose error (RPE), percentiles, confidence intervals that account for the temporal correlation of the deviations, and summary tables and HTML reports to compare several estimates.
  • Data: trajectopy, TUM, KITTI and EuRoC files, ASCII files with any column layout, Unix, date/time or GPS timestamps and any coordinate system (EPSG code), and ROS1 and ROS2 bags.
  • Visualization: fast, interactive plots (PNG, JPG or SVG export) and Google Earth export.
  • GUI: everything above without writing code, plus an interactive alignment for cases in which an automatic alignment fails.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
pip install "trajectopy[gui]"

Compute the absolute and relative trajectory error of an estimate. The example files are in the example_data folder of the repository.

import trajectopy as tpy

reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")

# ATE: the estimate is aligned to the reference first
ate_result = tpy.ate(estimate, reference)
print(ate_result)

# RPE: drift between poses 100 m to 800 m apart
rpe_result = tpy.rpe(estimate, reference)
print(rpe_result)

Or start the GUI with trajectopy, drop both files onto the trajectory table, right-click the reference and choose Set as Reference, then right-click the estimate and choose Compare with Reference → Absolute Error (ATE), with Alignment.

docs.title: API Policy
docs.text: This page describes what belongs to the public API of trajectopy, which conventions it follows and how it changes between releases.

docs.title: Public API
docs.text:
The public API consists of the names exported by these namespaces:

Namespace Content trajectopy Trajectories, settings, processing functions (alignment, matching, evaluation, ...), results, exceptions trajectopy.io Reading and writing of trajectories (trajectopy, TUM, KITTI and EuRoC files; reading of ROS bags), results, alignment parameters and KML files trajectopy.visualization Figures of trajectories, results and alignment parameters (needs trajectopy[plot]) trajectopy.exceptions The exceptions raised by trajectopy and its deprecation warning

Each of these namespaces lists its names in __all__. Everything else, for example trajectopy.core.trajectory, trajectopy.processing._lib, trajectopy.gui and trajectopy.cli, is an implementation detail. Such modules remain importable, but they can change in any release. Methods and attributes whose names start with an underscore are private as well.

import trajectopy as tpy
from trajectopy import io, visualization as vis

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
The whole public API follows the same conventions, so that it can grow without breaking changes:

  • Inputs are never modified. Functions and methods that transform a trajectory return a new object, and Trajectory copies the arrays it is created from. The keyword-only argument inplace=True modifies the input instead (and returns it, too). Always use the return value: trajectory = tpy.align(trajectory, reference). Exceptions are the methods Trajectory.set_sorting, ATEResult.set_sorting and ATEResult.remove_ate_above, which change the object itself.
  • One settings argument. Every processing function with settings takes a single settings argument, either of its own settings type (e.g. MatchingSettings) or the complete ProcessingSettings, from which it uses the part it needs. So the same ProcessingSettings can be passed to all of them. ate, which needs the matching and the alignment settings, takes only ProcessingSettings. None means the defaults.
  • Options accept strings. Options that are enumerations (e.g. MatchingMethod, Sorting) also accept their values as strings, e.g. MatchingSettings(method="nearest_temporal") or tpy.interpolate(trajectory, index, method="linear"); the lookup ignores the case. Options whose values are strings (e.g. the colormap of write_kml or the table_format of format_table) are written in lower case.
  • Keyword-only options. Only the data (trajectories, results, figures, file names, indices) and the settings are positional arguments; all options are keyword-only, so that new options can be added and options can be reordered without breaking calls. The constructors of data classes (the settings, the parameter sets, the deviations and Pose) take their fields as arguments, too.
  • Results carry everything. Results are returned as objects instead of tuples whose shape depends on a flag; for example, the alignment used by tpy.ate is available as ate_result.alignment. The only remaining exception is divide_into_laps(..., return_lap_indices=True).
  • Orientations are scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation objects.
  • Files. All functions that read or write files accept str and os.PathLike (e.g. pathlib.Path). Writers overwrite existing files; those with a mode argument append with mode="a". Only write_sensor_rotation_parameters and SensorRotationParameters.to_file always append (to an alignment result file).
  • Errors. Invalid arguments raise TypeError or ValueError. Errors specific to trajectopy raise the subclasses of trajectopy.TrajectopyError: TrajectoryError and PointSetError for trajectory and position data that do not fit together or cannot be transformed (e.g. a different number of positions and timestamps, an unknown EPSG code), TrajectopyIOError for files whose structure does not match their header or format (e.g. a wrong number of columns; values that cannot be parsed raise the ValueError of the parser), AlignmentError for alignments that cannot be estimated, AlignmentParametersError for invalid covariance matrices of alignment parameters and ApproximationError for failed approximations. TrajectopyIOError and AlignmentError are also ValueErrors. Errors of the file system (e.g. FileNotFoundError) are passed on unchanged, and trajectopy.visualization raises ImportError without the plotting extra.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
trajectopy follows semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.

  • Patch releases fix bugs.
  • Minor releases add functionality in a backwards compatible way and may deprecate parts of the API.
  • Major releases remove deprecated parts of the API. Other breaking changes are avoided.

The GUI and the command line interface are versioned together with the library.

docs.title: Deprecations
docs.text:
Parts of the public API are not removed without warning. They are first deprecated: they keep working, but emit a trajectopy.exceptions.TrajectopyDeprecationWarning (a subclass of DeprecationWarning) that names the replacement. Deprecated parts are removed in the next major release, at the earliest one minor release after the deprecation.

This policy applies from version 7 on. Version 7 itself removed the deprecated and redundant names of version 6 without a transition period; the release notes list their replacements.

To make sure that your code is ready for the next major release, turn the warnings into errors in your tests, e.g. with pytest:

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
filterwarnings = ["error::trajectopy.exceptions.TrajectopyDeprecationWarning"]

docs.title: Development Environment
docs.text:
Trajectopy uses uv for its development environment:

git clone https://github.com/gereon-t/trajectopy.git
cd trajectopy
uv sync --all-extras
uv run pre-commit install

The pre-commit hooks run before every commit: ruff (linting and formatting), the update of uv.lock and requirements.txt, mypy and the tests.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
uv run pytest

The tests cover the library, the GUI (without a display, with QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen), the command line and the documentation. Among others, they check that

  • the public API does not change unintentionally (test/test_public_api.py),
  • every public function, class, method and property has a complete docstring, every public name is in the API reference, every public function and class (except the exceptions) has examples, the examples of the documentation and of the docstrings run and show the actual output, and the scripts in example_scripts run (test/test_docs.py),
  • trajectopy itself does not use deprecated parts of its API (deprecation warnings are errors in the tests).

The CI checks formatting, linting and types, runs the tests on Linux and Windows with all supported Python versions (with a minimum test coverage of 85 %) and once without the plotting and GUI extras, and builds the documentation.

docs.title: Code Style
docs.text:
• Formatting and linting with ruff (line length 119), type checking with mypy.
  • Docstrings in the Google style, with Args, Returns and Raises sections, Examples that run as doctests (required for every public function and class except the exceptions) and, where helpful, See Also links written as [`trajectopy.ate`][trajectopy.ate].
  • Changes of the public API follow the API policy: new options are keyword-only, functions do not modify their inputs, and nothing is removed without a deprecation (trajectopy.utils.deprecation).
  • Every user-facing change is listed in CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is built with MkDocs and mkdocstrings from the folder trajectopy-docs:

cd trajectopy-docs
uv run mkdocs serve

The API reference is generated from the docstrings. Its pages in docs/api list the documented names; a new public name has to be added there (the tests check this). Examples in the user guide run in a folder that contains the example data of the repository (example_data) and a ROS2 bag (recording.mcap). An example that cannot run there is marked with <!-- skip-test: reason --> in the line before it. Printed output shown in a text block directly after an example is compared with the actual output.

mkdocs build --strict fails on broken links, anchors and references; the CI runs it for every change.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
1. Set the version in trajectopy/__version__.py and describe the changes in a section ## <version> of CHANGELOG.md (it is also the page Release Notes).
  2. Push the tag v<version>. The release workflow builds the apps for Windows, macOS and Linux and attaches them to the GitHub release of the tag, whose text is the section of the version in CHANGELOG.md. It fails if the tag does not match the version or the changelog has no section for it.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This tutorial evaluates the trajectories of two visual SLAM systems, ORB-SLAM and S-PTAM, against the ground truth of a KITTI sequence. It takes about ten minutes and introduces the concepts that the user guide explains in detail. The files are in the example_data folder of the repository; download them, or clone the repository, and run the examples in the folder that contains example_data.

Install trajectopy with the plotting extra first (see Installation):

pip install "trajectopy[plot]"

docs.title: 1. Load the Trajectories
docs.text:
A Trajectory holds timestamps, positions and orientations. The files contain a header that describes their columns; trajectopy also recognizes TUM, KITTI and EuRoC files.

import trajectopy as tpy

reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
orb = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
sptam = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_SPTAM.traj")
print(repr(orb))

<Trajectory 'KITTI ORB': 4541 poses with orientations, 3705.098 m, EPSG 0, sorted by time>

The trajectory has 4541 poses with orientations, it is 3.7 km long, its positions are given in a local coordinate system (EPSG code 0) and its poses are ordered by time. Its data are NumPy arrays:

print(orb.timestamps[:3], orb.xyz.shape)

[0. 1. 2.] (4541, 3)

docs.title: 2. Align the Estimate
docs.text:
A SLAM system starts in a coordinate frame of its own. Before its poses can be compared with the reference, the transformation between both frames is estimated: the alignment. By default, it is a rigid body transformation (translation and rotation), estimated by least squares from the corresponding poses (up to 5000 of them, see max_samples).

alignment = tpy.estimate_alignment(orb, reference)
translation = alignment.position_parameters
print(f"{translation.sim_trans_x.value:.3f} m, {translation.sim_trans_y.value:.3f} m, {translation.sim_trans_z.value:.3f} m")

aligned = tpy.apply_alignment(orb, alignment)

-1.363 m, 3.357 m, -0.328 m

Like every function of trajectopy, apply_alignment returns a new trajectory and leaves orb unchanged.

docs.title: 3. Absolute Trajectory Error
docs.text:
The absolute trajectory error (ATE) compares corresponding poses of the aligned estimate and the reference. ate matches the poses, aligns the estimate (as above) and computes the deviation of every pose:

ate_result = tpy.ate(orb, reference)
print(ate_result.describe()[["pos_mean", "pos_rms", "pos_max"]].round(3))

pos_mean    1.153
pos_rms     1.304
pos_max     3.638
Name: KITTI ORB vs. KITTI Ground Truth, dtype: float64

On average, the positions of ORB-SLAM deviate by 1.15 m from the reference. The result also holds the deviation of every pose, along the axes (pos_dev_x, …) and along the trajectory (pos_dev_along, pos_dev_cross_h, …).

docs.title: 4. Relative Pose Error
docs.text:
The relative pose error (RPE) measures the drift: how much the relative motion between poses that are, e.g., 100 m apart deviates from that of the reference. It needs no alignment.

rpe_result = tpy.rpe(orb, reference)
print(f"{rpe_result.pos_rpe:.3f} {rpe_result.pos_drift_unit}")

0.694 %

ORB-SLAM drifts by about 0.7 % of the distance travelled.

docs.title: 5. Compare Both Estimates
docs.text:
summary_table puts the statistics of several results side by side:

ate_results = [ate_result, tpy.ate(sptam, reference)]
table = tpy.summary_table(ate_results)
print(tpy.format_table(table[["pos_mean [m]", "pos_rms [m]"]], table_format="markdown", precision=3))

| name | pos_mean [m] | pos_rms [m] |
| --- | --- | --- |
| KITTI ORB vs. KITTI Ground Truth | 1.153 | 1.304 |
| KITTI SPTAM vs. KITTI Ground Truth | 3.489 | 3.739 |

docs.title: 6. Plot the Deviations
docs.text:
trajectopy.visualization creates the figures of the GUI. They are shown in an interactive window with vis.show(figures) or saved as images:

from trajectopy import visualization as vis

figures = vis.deviation_figures(ate_results, settings=tpy.PlotSettings(ate_unit_is_mm=True))
paths = vis.export_figures(figures, "plots")

docs.title: 7. Save the Results
docs.text:
Results and trajectories are saved as text files, which the GUI opens, too:

ate_result.to_file("orb_ate.result")
aligned.to_file("orb_aligned.traj")
tpy.write_report("report.html", ate_results, [rpe_result])

report.html is a self-contained report with all statistics and figures.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• The user guide explains trajectories, alignment, evaluation, plots and file formats in detail.
  • The GUI offers everything above without code: run trajectopy.
  • The command line evaluates trajectories in scripts and pipelines: trajectopy evaluate example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj --ref example_data/KITTI_gt.traj.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Trajectopy is available as a Python package and as a standalone app with the graphical user interface for Windows, macOS and Linux. The app is made for the GUI: it needs no Python installation, but offers no Python API, and the Windows app has no console output for the command line.

docs.title: Python Package
docs.text:
Trajectopy requires Python 3.10 or newer and is installed with pip. Choose the extras you need:

Command Contents pip install "trajectopy[gui]" Python package, plots and the GUI (recommended) pip install "trajectopy[plot]" Python package with plots (trajectopy.visualization), without the GUI pip install trajectopy Python package only: loading, alignment, evaluation and file I/O, no Qt pip install "trajectopy[fast]" Additionally reads large trajectory files several times faster (with pyarrow)

Extras can be combined, e.g. pip install "trajectopy[gui,fast]".

The installation provides the trajectopy command, which starts the GUI and offers commands for the command line.

To check the installation, print the versions of trajectopy and its dependencies:

import trajectopy as tpy

tpy.show_versions()

Please add this output to bug reports.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
pip install --upgrade "trajectopy[gui]"

Read the release notes before updating to a new major version: they list the changes that may require changes to your code.

docs.title: Apps
docs.text:
Every release provides

  • Trajectopy-<version>-setup.exe: installer for Windows,
  • Trajectopy-<version>-macos-arm64.dmg: app for macOS on Apple silicon,
  • Trajectopy-<version>-linux-x86_64.tar.gz: app for Linux (x86-64).

The apps are not signed; see below for what this means on each system.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Download Trajectopy-<version>-setup.exe from the latest release and run it. No Python installation or administrator rights are needed: the installer installs for the current user, or for all users if you choose so and confirm the administrator prompt. It adds Trajectopy to the Start menu and offers a desktop icon (off by default) and to open .traj and .tpy files with Trajectopy on double-click (on by default). The app reports new versions (Help → Check for Updates…); installing a newer version over an existing one updates it.

As the installer is not signed, Windows SmartScreen may warn about an unknown publisher: choose More info → Run anyway.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text: Open the .dmg and drag Trajectopy onto the Applications folder next to it. As the app is not signed, macOS refuses to open it at first: after the first attempt, allow it under System Settings → Privacy & Security with Open Anyway (on macOS 14 and older, right-click → Open works, too).

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Extract the archive and start the program Trajectopy in the extracted folder:

tar -xzf Trajectopy-<version>-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
./Trajectopy/Trajectopy

The app is built on Ubuntu 22.04 and runs on distributions with the same or a newer C library (glibc).

docs.title: Development Installation
docs.text: See Contributing for setting up a development environment.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to trajectopy from version 7 on are documented here. trajectopy follows semantic versioning; see the API policy for what is covered by it.

Version 7 settles the public API, so that it can grow without breaking changes. It defines which names are public, applies the same conventions to every function and removes deprecated and redundant names without a transition period: code of version 6 that uses them fails with an error. Changed defaults, above all that functions no longer modify their input, do not raise errors; they are listed under Breaking changes. The table of removed names and the migration guide below list the replacements.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Inputs are never modified by default. Every function and method with an inplace argument returns a new object unless inplace=True is passed. inplace is keyword-only.
  • One settings argument. All processing functions with settings take a single settings argument: their own settings type or the complete ProcessingSettings (ate takes only ProcessingSettings). The same settings object can be passed everywhere: tpy.ate(est, ref, settings), tpy.align(est, ref, settings), tpy.match_trajectories(est, ref, settings).
  • ate_result.alignment holds the alignment that was applied before the deviations were computed.
  • Options accept strings, e.g. tpy.MatchingSettings(method="nearest_temporal") or tpy.interpolate(trajectory, index, method="linear"), also when assigned to a setting (settings.matching.method = "nearest_temporal"). The lookup of these enumerations ignores the case.
  • Trajectory
  • accepts arrays in the constructor: tpy.Trajectory(xyz, quat, timestamps, name="...");
  • supports numpy-like indexing: trajectory[10] returns a tpy.Pose, trajectory[10:20], trajectory[mask] and trajectory[[0, 5]] return new trajectories;
  • has a one-line repr, equals(other, rtol=..., atol=...) and Trajectory.from_string;
  • writes all formats: trajectory.to_file("out.tum").
  • Results have one-line reprs and describe(): ATEResult.describe() returns the statistics as a pandas.Series, RPEResult.describe() the drift statistics per pair distance as a pandas.DataFrame.
  • File I/O: all reading and writing functions accept pathlib.Path. trajectopy.io.read_trajectory and write_trajectory handle all formats (trajectopy, TUM, KITTI, EuRoC); trajectopy.io also exports TrajectoryFormat, detect_format, read_tum, read_kitti, read_euroc, list_topics and trajectories_from_rosbag.
  • Public API: the names exported by trajectopy, trajectopy.io, trajectopy.visualization and trajectopy.exceptions form the public API, guarded by a test. New: tpy.Pose, tpy.adopt_first_pose, tpy.show_versions and trajectopy.exceptions.TrajectopyDeprecationWarning. The types that results consist of are public and documented, too: tpy.AbsoluteTrajectoryDeviations (ATEResult.abs_dev), tpy.RelativeTrajectoryDeviations (RPEResult.rpe_dev), tpy.ComponentCorrelation (DeviationCorrelation.components), tpy.HelmertTransformation and tpy.Leverarm (AlignmentParameters.helmert, .leverarm) and trajectopy.visualization.SpeedFit.
  • trajectopy attaches a NullHandler to its logger and leaves the logging configuration to applications.

docs.title: New Features
docs.text:
Besides the API changes above, version 7 adds:

  • GUI: an interactive alignment window (drag, point pairs, time synchronization, diagnosis of the alignment parameters and least squares refinement), which replaces the manual alignment window; export of HTML reports and summary tables; a faster file dialog on Windows; and a System entry in the Theme menu, which follows the color scheme of the operating system. The chosen theme is kept for the next start.
  • Command line: the commands ate, rpe, evaluate, align, convert and info evaluate, align and convert trajectories without the GUI.
  • Evaluation: percentiles (pos_dev_percentile), confidence intervals that account for correlated deviations (confidence_interval), statistics per segment (segment_statistics), summary tables of several results (summary_table, format_table) and self-contained HTML reports (write_report).
  • Plots: ate_boxplot_figure.
  • File formats: TUM, KITTI and EuRoC files are read (recognized automatically, with a log message) and written; ROS2 bags are also read from single .mcap and .db3 files, and besides PoseStamped and PointStamped, poses with covariance, odometry, transforms, paths and GNSS fixes are read.
  • Alignment: positions are weighted by their standard deviations (Trajectory.position_std, read from ROS covariances and the sx, sy, sz columns of trajectopy files).

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
Compared with version 6.2.1. A script compared the public API of both versions name by name and parameter by parameter; every difference that can break existing code is listed here.

Functions no longer modify their input by default

  • inplace is keyword-only everywhere and defaults to False, so that the input is left unchanged and the result is returned. It defaulted to True for Trajectory.crop, Trajectory.intersect, Trajectory.mask, Trajectory.transform, Positions.to_epsg, Positions.to_local, align, apply_alignment, interpolate, match_trajectories and sort_spatially; it was positional for these and for approximate and Positions.mean.

One settings argument

  • estimate_alignment, align, ate, rpe, match_trajectories, sort_spatially and approximate take a single settings argument instead of alignment_settings, matching_settings, processing_settings, sorting_settings and approximation_settings (see the table below).

Options are keyword-only

Only the data (trajectories, results, figures, file names, indices) and the settings are positional arguments. The following arguments must now be passed by keyword:

  • Processing: estimate_alignment(initial_parameters=), ate(align=), interpolate(method=, max_gap_size=), divide_into_laps(return_lap_indices=).
  • Trajectory(name=, path_lengths=, velocity_xyz=, sorting=), Trajectory.crop(inverse=), Trajectory.intersect(max_gap_size=), Trajectory.to_file(mode=), Trajectory.to_kml(precision=, color=), Trajectory.to_dataframe(sort_by=).
  • Positions(local_transformer=, init_local_transformer=, epsg_local_cart=, epsg_local_geod=).
  • Results: ATEResult(name=), RPEResult(name=), all fields of AlignmentResult, ATEResult.to_file(mode=), RPEResult.to_file(mode=), ATEResult.to_kml(field=, max_std=), RPEResult.compute_metric(factor=), DeviationCorrelation.from_ate_result(max_lag=, window=).
  • Parameters and settings: Parameter(default=, enabled=, name=, unit=); enabled_only (and lower_case) of get_covariance_matrix, to_dict, to_string_list, to_name_list and AlignmentParameters.params_labels; AlignmentEstimationSettings.from_components(similarity=, time_shift=, leverarm=, sensor_rotation=) and AlignmentEstimationSettings.all(sensor_rotation=).
  • trajectopy.io: write_trajectory(mode=), write_ate_result(mode=), write_rpe_result(mode=) and all options of write_kml and write_ate_kml (color, field, colormap, max_std, value_range, color_classes, heights, height_offset, extrude, line_width, precision).
  • trajectopy.visualization: Figure.export(variant=, width=), Figure.create_widget(use_opengl=), PlotWindow(title=, export_format=, export_width=, use_opengl=, parent=), export_figures(export_format=, width=), show(title=, block=, use_opengl=), set_theme(dark=), ate_speed_figure(speed_window=), parameter_matrix_figure(correlation=), smoothed_speed(window=).

Changed behavior

  • ATEResult.to_file, RPEResult.to_file and AlignmentResult.to_file (and trajectopy.io.write_ate_result, write_rpe_result and write_alignment_result) overwrite existing files instead of appending to them; pass mode="a" to append.
  • ate(..., align=False) sets ate_result.alignment to None.
  • trajectopy.io.read_trajectory and Trajectory.from_file recognize TUM, KITTI and EuRoC files; write_trajectory and Trajectory.to_file choose the format from the file extension (.tum, .kitti) and write the trajectopy format otherwise.
  • Orientations are scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation objects: trajectory.rotations, ATEResult.abs_dev.rot_dev, AlignmentParameters.helmert.rotation_set and SensorRotationParameters.rotation_set. The Rotations class (a subclass of scipy's Rotation) and its module trajectopy.core.rotations are gone. Compose rotations with * and inv() instead of + and - (a - b is a * b.inv()), and use magnitude() instead of rotangle.
  • repr(trajectory) is a one-line summary; str(trajectory) still prints the summary table.
  • The alignment weights the positions by their standard deviations (AlignmentStochastics.use_position_std, True by default). Alignments of trajectories with standard deviations (the sx, sy, sz columns of trajectopy files or the covariances of ROS messages) therefore differ from version 6, which ignored them; set use_position_std=False for the results of version 6.
  • Trajectories read from files without a #name line are named after the file (e.g. estimate for estimate.traj) instead of Trajectory; the names of results (<trajectory> vs. <reference>) change accordingly.
  • Invalid values in settings files (e.g. an unknown matching method) raise TypeError instead of ValueError.
  • Options are converted with str() to their value, e.g. str(tpy.Sorting.TIME) == "time".
  • File contents that do not match their header or format raise TrajectopyIOError and alignments that cannot be estimated raise AlignmentError (both are also ValueErrors, see Fixes).

Removed names and modules

  • The names and arguments in the table Removed and renamed names below.
  • The modules deprecated since version 5: trajectopy.readers (use trajectopy.io), trajectopy.utils.common and trajectopy.processing.lib.alignment.parameters (use trajectopy.AlignmentParameters).
  • The internal package trajectopy.processing.lib was renamed to trajectopy.processing._lib to mark it as private.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• The documentation is restructured: installation, a user guide with one page per topic (trajectories, alignment, evaluation, visualization, Google Earth, file formats, settings, GUI, command line), an API reference organized by the public namespaces, the API policy and the release notes.
  • Every public function, class, method and property is documented with its arguments and return value. Every public function and class (except the exceptions) has examples, which run as doctests; many link to related functions (See Also).
  • The examples of the user guide and the scripts in example_scripts are run by the tests.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• trajectopy.match_trajectories failed with an import error if it was the first processing function used in a session.
  • AlignmentParameters.to_file (and trajectopy.io.write_alignment_parameters) wrote files that AlignmentParameters.from_file could not read; the parameters are now written with their enabled flags and 17 significant digits.
  • An unknown #time_format in a file header raises a TrajectopyIOError that lists the valid formats instead of a KeyError.
  • TrajectopyIOError and AlignmentError are raised now: for files whose structure does not match their header or format (e.g. a wrong number of columns) and for alignments that cannot be estimated (e.g. no poses left after the preprocessing), where a plain ValueError was raised before. Both are also ValueErrors, so existing error handling keeps working.
  • Trajectory(..., sorting=), Trajectory.set_sorting and ATEResult.set_sorting accept the sorting as a string ("time", "path_length", case-insensitive), like all other options; before, a string broke the repr and the file export of the trajectory.
  • Positions.mean(inplace=True) returns the modified object, like all other functions with inplace.
  • Trajectory(...) copies the arrays and the Positions object it is created from; before, it reordered the caller's positions in place when the timestamps were not in chronological order.
  • The poses returned when iterating over a trajectory hold their velocity as a tuple, like those returned by indexing; before, it was a NumPy array, so that comparing poses failed.
  • Alignment result files keep whether the estimation converged (#converged false); before, every alignment read from a file counted as converged.

docs.text: Version 6 Version 7 estimate_alignment(..., alignment_settings=, matching_settings=), same for align settings= (AlignmentSettings or ProcessingSettings) ate(..., processing_settings=), rpe(..., processing_settings=) settings= match_trajectories(..., matching_settings=) settings= sort_spatially(..., sorting_settings=) settings= approximate(..., approximation_settings=) settings= ate(..., return_alignment=True) ate_result.alignment Trajectory.from_file(text, io_stream=True) Trajectory.from_string(text) trajectopy.IOError, trajectopy.exceptions.IOError trajectopy.TrajectopyIOError trajectopy.ComparisonMethod none (an internal detail of the file I/O) trajectopy.io.HeaderData none (an internal detail of reading files) MatchingMethod.UNKNOWN none (it was never a matching method); settings files with "method": "unknown" can no longer be read trajectopy.Rotations scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation

docs.title: Migrating from version 6
docs.text:
# version 6
aligned = tpy.align(est, ref, alignment_settings=s.alignment, matching_settings=s.matching)  # modified est
ate_result, alignment = tpy.ate(est, ref, processing_settings=s, return_alignment=True)
trajectory.crop(10, 20)  # modified trajectory

# version 7
aligned = tpy.align(est, ref, s)  # est is unchanged
ate_result = tpy.ate(est, ref, s)
alignment = ate_result.alignment
trajectory = trajectory.crop(10, 20)  # or trajectory.crop(10, 20, inplace=True)

Code that relied on functions modifying their input without using the return value has to use the return value (or pass inplace=True). Removed arguments raise a TypeError and removed names an AttributeError (an ImportError with from ... import).

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
This reference describes the public API of trajectopy: the names of the namespaces trajectopy, trajectopy.io, trajectopy.visualization and trajectopy.exceptions. Import them from these namespaces; the API policy describes the conventions of the API and which changes to expect between versions.

import trajectopy as tpy
from trajectopy import io, visualization as vis

Pose A single pose of a trajectory, as returned by indexing a trajectory with an integer or iterating over it. Positions Class representing (georeferenced) positions.

docs.title: Processing

docs.title: ate
docs.text:
ate(
    trajectory: Trajectory,
    other: Trajectory,
    settings: ProcessingSettings | None = None,
    *,
    align: bool = True,
) -> ATEResult

Computes the absolute trajectory error (ATE) between two trajectories.

The ATE is computed by first matching the estimated trajectory to the ground truth trajectory. Then, the alignment between the two trajectories is estimated. The estimated trajectory is aligned to the ground truth trajectory using the estimated alignment. Finally, the ATE is computed by comparing the aligned estimated trajectory to the ground truth trajectory.

Parameters:

  • trajectory (Trajectory) –

    Trajectory to be evaluated.

  • other (Trajectory) –

    Ground truth trajectory.

  • settings (ProcessingSettings, default: None ) –

    Processing settings, of which the matching and alignment settings are used. Defaults to the default settings.

  • align (bool, default: True ) –

    Whether to align the trajectory before computing the deviations. Defaults to True.

Returns:

  • ATEResult ( ATEResult ) –

    Result of the ATE computation. Its attribute alignment holds the estimated alignment

  • ATEResult –

    (None with align=False).

See Also

trajectopy.rpe: drift instead of absolute deviations. trajectopy.ATEResult: the result. trajectopy.visualization.deviation_figures: plots of the result.

References
  1. J. Sturm, N. Engelhard, F. Endres, W. Burgard, D. Cremers (2012): A benchmark for the evaluation of RGB-D SLAM systems. IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS).
  2. G. Tombrink, A. Dreier, L. Klingbeil, H. Kuhlmann (2024): Spatio-temporal trajectory alignment for trajectory evaluation. Journal of Applied Geodesy. https://doi.org/10.1515/jag-2024-0040

Examples:

>>> import trajectopy as tpy
>>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
>>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
>>> ate_result = tpy.ate(estimate, reference)
>>> print(f"{ate_result.pos_ate:.3f} m")
1.153 m
>>> ate_result.alignment.converged
True
Source code in trajectopy\processing\evaluation.py 
def ate(
    trajectory: Trajectory,
    other: Trajectory,
    settings: ProcessingSettings | None = None,
    *,
    align: bool = True,
) -> ATEResult:
    """Computes the absolute trajectory error (ATE) between two trajectories.

    The ATE is computed by first matching the estimated trajectory to the ground truth trajectory.
    Then, the alignment between the two trajectories is estimated. The estimated trajectory is
    aligned to the ground truth trajectory using the estimated alignment. Finally, the ATE is
    computed by comparing the aligned estimated trajectory to the ground truth trajectory.

    Args:
        trajectory (Trajectory): Trajectory to be evaluated.
        other (Trajectory): Ground truth trajectory.
        settings (ProcessingSettings, optional): Processing settings, of which the matching and alignment
            settings are used. Defaults to the default settings.
        align (bool, optional): Whether to align the trajectory before computing the deviations.
            Defaults to True.

    Returns:
        ATEResult: Result of the ATE computation. Its attribute ``alignment`` holds the estimated alignment
        (None with ``align=False``).

    See Also:
        [`trajectopy.rpe`][trajectopy.rpe]: drift instead of absolute deviations.
        [`trajectopy.ATEResult`][trajectopy.ATEResult]: the result.
        [`trajectopy.visualization.deviation_figures`][trajectopy.visualization.deviation_figures]: plots of the result.

    References:
        1. J. Sturm, N. Engelhard, F. Endres, W. Burgard, D. Cremers (2012): A benchmark for the evaluation of RGB-D SLAM systems. IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS).
        2. G. Tombrink, A. Dreier, L. Klingbeil, H. Kuhlmann (2024): Spatio-temporal trajectory alignment for trajectory evaluation. Journal of Applied Geodesy. https://doi.org/10.1515/jag-2024-0040

    Examples:
        >>> import trajectopy as tpy
        >>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
        >>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
        >>> ate_result = tpy.ate(estimate, reference)
        >>> print(f"{ate_result.pos_ate:.3f} m")
        1.153 m
        >>> ate_result.alignment.converged
        True
    """
    processing = resolve_settings(settings, ProcessingSettings)

    trajectory, other = match_trajectories(trajectory, other, processing.matching)

    alignment: AlignmentResult | None = None
    if align:
        alignment = estimate_alignment(trajectory, other, processing)
        trajectory = apply_alignment(trajectory, alignment)

    result = _compare_trajectories_absolute(other=other, trajectory=trajectory)
    result.alignment = alignment
    return result

docs.text:
rpe(
    trajectory: Trajectory,
    other: Trajectory,
    settings: ProcessingSettings
    | RelativeComparisonSettings
    | None = None,
) -> RPEResult

Computes the relative pose error (RPE) between two trajectories.

The RPE is computed by comparing the relative poses between the estimated and ground truth trajectories. The pose distances are either defined in meters or in seconds depending on the settings.

Parameters:

  • trajectory (Trajectory) –

    Trajectory to be evaluated.

  • other (Trajectory) –

    Ground truth trajectory.

  • settings (ProcessingSettings | RelativeComparisonSettings, default: None ) –

    Relative comparison settings, or processing settings whose matching and relative comparison settings are used. Defaults to the default settings.

Returns:

  • RPEResult ( RPEResult ) –

    Result of the RPE computation.

See Also

trajectopy.ate: absolute deviations. trajectopy.RPEResult: the result. trajectopy.RelativeComparisonSettings: the pair distances.

References
  1. J. Sturm, N. Engelhard, F. Endres, W. Burgard, D. Cremers (2012): A benchmark for the evaluation of RGB-D SLAM systems. IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS).
  2. A. Geiger, P. Lenz, R. Urtasun (2012): Are we ready for autonomous driving? The KITTI vision benchmark suite. IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR).

Examples:

>>> import trajectopy as tpy
>>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
>>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
>>> rpe_result = tpy.rpe(estimate, reference)
>>> round(rpe_result.pos_rpe, 3), rpe_result.pos_drift_unit
(0.694, '%')
Source code in trajectopy\processing\evaluation.py 
def rpe(
    trajectory: Trajectory,
    other: Trajectory,
    settings: ProcessingSettings | RelativeComparisonSettings | None = None,
) -> RPEResult:
    """Computes the relative pose error (RPE) between two trajectories.

    The RPE is computed by comparing the relative poses between the estimated and ground truth
    trajectories. The pose distances are either defined in meters or in seconds depending on
    the settings.

    Args:
        trajectory (Trajectory): Trajectory to be evaluated.
        other (Trajectory): Ground truth trajectory.
        settings (ProcessingSettings | RelativeComparisonSettings, optional): Relative comparison settings,
            or processing settings whose matching and relative comparison settings are used. Defaults to the
            default settings.

    Returns:
        RPEResult: Result of the RPE computation.

    See Also:
        [`trajectopy.ate`][trajectopy.ate]: absolute deviations.
        [`trajectopy.RPEResult`][trajectopy.RPEResult]: the result.
        [`trajectopy.RelativeComparisonSettings`][trajectopy.RelativeComparisonSettings]: the pair distances.

    References:
        1. J. Sturm, N. Engelhard, F. Endres, W. Burgard, D. Cremers (2012): A benchmark for the evaluation of RGB-D SLAM systems. IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS).
        2. A. Geiger, P. Lenz, R. Urtasun (2012): Are we ready for autonomous driving? The KITTI vision benchmark suite. IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR).

    Examples:
        >>> import trajectopy as tpy
        >>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
        >>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
        >>> rpe_result = tpy.rpe(estimate, reference)
        >>> round(rpe_result.pos_rpe, 3), rpe_result.pos_drift_unit
        (0.694, '%')
    """
    if isinstance(settings, RelativeComparisonSettings):
        matching, relative_comparison = MatchingSettings(), settings
    else:
        processing = resolve_settings(settings, ProcessingSettings)
        matching, relative_comparison = processing.matching, processing.relative_comparison

    trajectory, other = match_trajectories(trajectory, other, matching)
    return _compare_trajectories_relative(
        trajectory=trajectory,
        other=other,
        relative_comparison_settings=relative_comparison,
    )

docs.title: summary_table
docs.text:
summary_table(
    ate_results: Sequence[ATEResult] = (),
    rpe_results: Sequence[RPEResult] = (),
    *,
    confidence_intervals: bool = True,
) -> DataFrame

ATE and RPE summaries side by side, joined by the result names (outer join, so that results with only an ATE or only an RPE keep their row).

The columns of the ATE results are poses (number of matched poses), pos_mean [m], pos_median [m], pos_rms [m], pos_std [m], pos_p95 [m] (95th percentile) and pos_max [m] of the position deviations; with confidence_intervals, the 95% confidence intervals of the mean and the RMS (pos_mean_ci_low [m], pos_mean_ci_high [m], pos_rms_ci_low [m], pos_rms_ci_high [m], see ATEResult.confidence_interval); and rot_mean [deg], rot_rms [deg], rot_p95 [deg] and rot_max [deg] of the rotation deviations (NaN without orientations). The columns of the RPE results are pose_pairs, pos_drift and rot_drift (averages over all pair distances, the latter in degrees) with their units pos_drift_unit (% or m/s) and rot_drift_unit (deg/100m or deg/s).

Parameters:

  • ate_results (Sequence[ATEResult], default: () ) –

    ATE results.

  • rpe_results (Sequence[RPEResult], default: () ) –

    RPE results, named like the corresponding ATE results.

  • confidence_intervals (bool, default: True ) –

    Add the confidence intervals (slower). Defaults to True.

Returns:

  • DataFrame –

    pd.DataFrame: One row per name, indexed by the names (duplicates get a suffix).

See Also

trajectopy.format_table: writes the table as text. trajectopy.write_report: an HTML report.

Examples:

>>> import trajectopy as tpy
>>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
>>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
>>> ate_result = tpy.ate(estimate, reference)
>>> table = tpy.summary_table([ate_result])
>>> print(tpy.format_table(table[["poses", "pos_mean [m]"]], table_format="markdown", precision=3))
| name | poses | pos_mean [m] |
| --- | --- | --- |
| KITTI ORB vs. KITTI Ground Truth | 4541 | 1.153 |
Source code in trajectopy\results\summary.py 
def summary_table(
    ate_results: Sequence[ATEResult] = (),
    rpe_results: Sequence[RPEResult] = (),
    *,
    confidence_intervals: bool = True,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """ATE and RPE summaries side by side, joined by the result names (outer join, so that results with only an
    ATE or only an RPE keep their row).

    The columns of the ATE results are ``poses`` (number of matched poses), ``pos_mean [m]``,
    ``pos_median [m]``, ``pos_rms [m]``, ``pos_std [m]``, ``pos_p95 [m]`` (95th percentile) and ``pos_max [m]`` of
    the position deviations; with ``confidence_intervals``, the 95% confidence intervals of the mean and the RMS
    (``pos_mean_ci_low [m]``, ``pos_mean_ci_high [m]``, ``pos_rms_ci_low [m]``, ``pos_rms_ci_high [m]``, see
    [`ATEResult.confidence_interval`][trajectopy.ATEResult.confidence_interval]); and ``rot_mean [deg]``, ``rot_rms [deg]``, ``rot_p95 [deg]`` and
    ``rot_max [deg]`` of the rotation deviations (NaN without orientations). The columns of the RPE results are
    ``pose_pairs``, ``pos_drift`` and ``rot_drift`` (averages over all pair distances, the latter in degrees)
    with their units ``pos_drift_unit`` (``%`` or ``m/s``) and ``rot_drift_unit`` (``deg/100m`` or ``deg/s``).

    Args:
        ate_results (Sequence[ATEResult], optional): ATE results.
        rpe_results (Sequence[RPEResult], optional): RPE results, named like the corresponding ATE results.
        confidence_intervals (bool, optional): Add the confidence intervals (slower). Defaults to True.

    Returns:
        pd.DataFrame: One row per name, indexed by the names (duplicates get a suffix).

    See Also:
        [`trajectopy.format_table`][trajectopy.format_table]: writes the table as text.
        [`trajectopy.write_report`][trajectopy.write_report]: an HTML report.

    Examples:
        >>> import trajectopy as tpy
        >>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
        >>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
        >>> ate_result = tpy.ate(estimate, reference)
        >>> table = tpy.summary_table([ate_result])
        >>> print(tpy.format_table(table[["poses", "pos_mean [m]"]], table_format="markdown", precision=3))
        | name | poses | pos_mean [m] |
        | --- | --- | --- |
        | KITTI ORB vs. KITTI Ground Truth | 4541 | 1.153 |
        <BLANKLINE>
    """
    ate = ate_summary(ate_results, confidence_intervals) if ate_results else pd.DataFrame()
    rpe = rpe_summary(rpe_results) if rpe_results else pd.DataFrame()
    if ate.empty:
        return rpe
    if rpe.empty:
        return ate
    table = ate.join(rpe, how="outer")
    # counts stay integers, also where the outer join left them empty
    for column in ("poses", "pose_pairs"):
        table[column] = table[column].astype("Int64")
    return table

def format_table(table: pd.DataFrame, *, table_format: str = "csv", precision: int = 4) -> str:
    """Formats a summary table as CSV, Markdown or LaTeX (without additional dependencies).

    Args:
        table (pd.DataFrame): Table, e.g. from [`summary_table`][trajectopy.summary_table].
        table_format (str, optional): ``csv``, ``markdown`` or ``latex``. Defaults to ``csv``.
        precision (int, optional): Number of decimals of floats. Defaults to 4.

    Returns:
        str: The formatted table.

    See Also:
        [`trajectopy.summary_table`][trajectopy.summary_table]: creates the table.

    Examples:
        >>> import trajectopy as tpy
        >>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
        >>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
        >>> ate_result = tpy.ate(estimate, reference)
        >>> table = tpy.summary_table([ate_result])
        >>> print(tpy.format_table(table[["poses"]], table_format="csv"))
        name,poses
        KITTI ORB vs. KITTI Ground Truth,4541
        <BLANKLINE>
    """
    if table_format not in TABLE_FORMATS:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown table format '{table_format}'. Options: {', '.join(TABLE_FORMATS)}.")
    if table_format == "csv":
        return table.to_csv(float_format=f"%.{precision}f")

    header = [str(table.index.name or ""), *map(str, table.columns)]
    rows = [[str(name), *values] for name, values in zip(table.index, formatted(table, precision).to_numpy())]

    if table_format == "markdown":
        lines = ["| " + " | ".join(header) + " |", "|" + "|".join(" --- " for _ in header) + "|"]
        lines += ["| " + " | ".join(row) + " |" for row in rows]
        return "\n".join(lines) + "\n"

    def escape(text: str) -> str:
        for char in ("\\", "&", "%", "$", "#", "_", "{", "}"):
            text = text.replace(char, "\\" + char)
        return text

    lines = [
        "\\begin{tabular}{l" + "r" * len(table.columns) + "}",
        "\\hline",
        " & ".join(escape(text) for text in header) + " \\\\",
        "\\hline",
        *(" & ".join(escape(text) for text in row) + " \\\\" for row in rows),
        "\\hline",
        "\\end{tabular}",
    ]
    return "\n".join(lines) + "\n"

docs.title: Exceptions and Warnings
docs.text: All exceptions defined by trajectopy derive from TrajectopyError; the exception classes are also available in the trajectopy namespace (except the warning). Besides them, invalid arguments raise the built-in TypeError or ValueError, and errors of the file system (e.g. FileNotFoundError) are passed on unchanged. The API policy says which exception is raised when.

def read_trajectory(
    filename: str | os.PathLike,
    *,
    format: "str | TrajectoryFormat" = TrajectoryFormat.AUTO,  # noqa: A002
) -> Trajectory:
    """Reads a trajectory file in any supported format.

    Args:
        filename (str | os.PathLike): Path to the file.
        format (str | TrajectoryFormat, optional): One of ``auto``, ``trajectopy``, ``tum``, ``kitti`` and
            ``euroc``. With ``auto`` (default), the format is recognized by [`detect_format`][trajectopy.io.detect_format].

    Returns:
        Trajectory: The loaded trajectory.

    See Also:
        [`trajectopy.Trajectory.from_file`][trajectopy.Trajectory.from_file]: the same as a class method.
        [`trajectopy.io.write_trajectory`][trajectopy.io.write_trajectory]: writes trajectories.

    Examples:
        >>> from trajectopy import io
        >>> trajectory = io.read_trajectory("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
        >>> io.write_trajectory(trajectory, "poses.txt", format="kitti")
        >>> io.detect_format("poses.txt")
        <TrajectoryFormat.KITTI: 'kitti'>
        >>> len(io.read_trajectory("poses.txt"))
        4541
    """
    from trajectopy.io import trajectory_io

    filename = os.fspath(filename)
    file_format = TrajectoryFormat(format)
    if file_format == TrajectoryFormat.AUTO:
        file_format, has_fields = _scan_format(filename)
        if file_format != TrajectoryFormat.TRAJECTOPY:
            logger.info("Recognized %s as a %s file.", filename, _DISPLAY_NAMES[file_format])
        elif not has_fields:
            logger.info(
                "%s has no #fields header: its columns are read as t,px,py,pz,qx,qy,qz,qw (TUM format).", filename
            )

    if file_format == TrajectoryFormat.TRAJECTOPY:
        return trajectory_io.read_trajectory(filename, default_name=_name(filename))
    readers: dict[TrajectoryFormat, Callable[[str], Trajectory]] = {
        TrajectoryFormat.TUM: read_tum,
        TrajectoryFormat.KITTI: read_kitti,
        TrajectoryFormat.EUROC: read_euroc,
    }
    return readers[file_format](filename)

def write_trajectory(
    trajectory: Trajectory,
    filename: str | os.PathLike,
    *,
    format: "str | TrajectoryFormat" = TrajectoryFormat.AUTO,  # noqa: A002
    mode: str = "w",
) -> None:
    """Writes a trajectory in one of the supported formats.

    Args:
        trajectory (Trajectory): Trajectory to write.
        filename (str | os.PathLike): Output path.
        format (str | TrajectoryFormat, optional): One of ``auto`` (default), ``trajectopy``, ``tum``,
            ``kitti`` and ``euroc``. ``auto`` picks the format from the file extension (``.tum``, ``.kitti``)
            and writes trajectopy files otherwise.
        mode (str, optional): ``"w"`` (default) overwrites the file, ``"a"`` appends to it.

    See Also:
        [`trajectopy.io.read_trajectory`][trajectopy.io.read_trajectory]: reads all formats.

    Examples:
        >>> from trajectopy import io
        >>> trajectory = io.read_trajectory("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
        >>> io.write_trajectory(trajectory, "poses.tum")  # format from the extension
        >>> io.write_trajectory(trajectory, "poses.csv", format="euroc")
    """
    from trajectopy.io import trajectory_io

    filename = os.fspath(filename)
    file_format = TrajectoryFormat(format)
    if file_format == TrajectoryFormat.AUTO:
        suffixes = {".tum": TrajectoryFormat.TUM, ".kitti": TrajectoryFormat.KITTI}
        file_format = suffixes.get(Path(filename).suffix.lower(), TrajectoryFormat.TRAJECTOPY)

    if file_format == TrajectoryFormat.TRAJECTOPY:
        trajectory_io.write_trajectory(trajectory, filename, mode=mode)
        return

    writers = {
        TrajectoryFormat.TUM: to_tum_string,
        TrajectoryFormat.KITTI: to_kitti_string,
        TrajectoryFormat.EUROC: to_euroc_string,
    }
    with open(filename, mode, newline="\n", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        file.write(writers[file_format](trajectory))

def detect_format(filename: str | os.PathLike) -> TrajectoryFormat:

def read_tum(filename: str | os.PathLike, *, name: str = "") -> Trajectory:
    """Reads a trajectory in the TUM format (``timestamp tx ty tz qx qy qz qw``).

    Args:
        filename (str): Path to the file.
        name (str, optional): Name of the trajectory. Defaults to the file name.

    Returns:
        Trajectory: The trajectory, in a local coordinate system (EPSG 0).

    See Also:
        [`trajectopy.io.read_trajectory`][trajectopy.io.read_trajectory]: recognizes the format.

    Examples:
        >>> from trajectopy import io
        >>> io.write_trajectory(io.read_trajectory("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj"), "poses.tum")
        >>> len(io.read_tum("poses.tum", name="KITTI"))
        4541
    """
    filename = os.fspath(filename)
    data = _numeric_table(filename, delimiter=None)
    if data.ndim != 2 or data.shape[1] < 8:
        raise TrajectopyIOError(
            f"A TUM file has 8 columns (timestamp tx ty tz qx qy qz qw), {filename} has {data.shape[-1]}."
        )
    return Trajectory(
        positions=Positions(xyz=data[:, 1:4]),
        rotations=Rotation.from_quat(data[:, 4:8]),
        timestamps=data[:, 0],
        name=name or _name(filename),
    )

def read_kitti(
    filename: str | os.PathLike, *, timestamps: np.ndarray | str | None = None, name: str = ""
) -> Trajectory:
    """Reads a trajectory in the KITTI odometry format (one row-major 3x4 pose matrix per line).

    Args:
        filename (str): Path to the file.
        timestamps (np.ndarray | str | None, optional): Timestamps of the poses, or the path to a file with one
            timestamp per line (KITTI's ``times.txt``). Without them, the poses are numbered 0, 1, 2, ...
        name (str, optional): Name of the trajectory. Defaults to the file name.

    Returns:
        Trajectory: The trajectory, in a local coordinate system (EPSG 0).

    See Also:
        [`trajectopy.io.read_trajectory`][trajectopy.io.read_trajectory]: recognizes the format.

    Examples:
        >>> from trajectopy import io
        >>> trajectory = io.read_trajectory("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
        >>> io.write_trajectory(trajectory, "poses.txt", format="kitti")
        >>> io.read_kitti("poses.txt").timestamps[:3]  # numbered without timestamps
        array([0., 1., 2.])
    """
    filename = os.fspath(filename)
    data = _numeric_table(filename, delimiter=None)
    if data.ndim != 2 or data.shape[1] != _KITTI_COLUMNS:
        raise TrajectopyIOError(
            f"A KITTI file has 12 values per line (3x4 pose matrix), {filename} has {data.shape[-1]}."
        )

    matrices = data.reshape(-1, 3, 4)
    if isinstance(timestamps, str | Path):
        timestamps = np.loadtxt(timestamps, comments="#", ndmin=1)
    if timestamps is not None and len(timestamps) != len(matrices):
        raise ValueError(f"{len(timestamps)} timestamps were given for {len(matrices)} poses.")

    return Trajectory(
        positions=Positions(xyz=matrices[:, :, 3].copy()),
        rotations=Rotation.from_matrix(matrices[:, :, :3]),
        timestamps=None if timestamps is None else np.asarray(timestamps, dtype=float),
        name=name or _name(filename),
    )

    if data.ndim != 2 or data.shape[1] < 8:
        raise TrajectopyIOError(
            f"A EuRoC file has at least 8 columns (timestamp, position, quaternion), {filename} has {data.shape[-1]}."
        )
    return Trajectory(
        positions=Positions(xyz=data[:, 1:4]),
        rotations=Rotation.from_quat(data[:, [5, 6, 7, 4]]),
        timestamps=data[:, 0] * 1e-9,
        velocity_xyz=data[:, 8:11] if data.shape[1] >= 11 else None,
        name=name or _name(filename),
    )

def trajectory_to_string(trajectory: Trajectory) -> str:
    """Returns a trajectory in the trajectopy ASCII format, as [`write_trajectory`][trajectopy.io.write_trajectory] writes it.

    The header contains the EPSG code, the name, the navigation frame (always ENU), the sorting and the
    fields ``t,l,px,py,pz,qx,qy,qz,qw,vx,vy,vz`` (without the quaternion for trajectories without
    orientations, followed by ``sx,sy,sz`` for trajectories with position standard deviations).

    Args:
        trajectory (Trajectory): Trajectory to convert.

    Returns:
        str: Content of a trajectory file.

    Examples:
        >>> from trajectopy import io
        >>> trajectory = io.read_trajectory("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
        >>> io.trajectory_to_string(trajectory).splitlines()[4]
        '#fields t,l,px,py,pz,qx,qy,qz,qw,vx,vy,vz'
    """
    fields = "t,l,px,py,pz,vx,vy,vz" if trajectory.rotations is None else "t,l,px,py,pz,qx,qy,qz,qw,vx,vy,vz"
    if trajectory.position_std is not None:
        fields += ",sx,sy,sz"
    header = [
        f"#epsg {trajectory.positions.epsg}",
        f"#name {trajectory.name}",
        "#nframe enu",
        f"#sorting {trajectory.sorting.value}",
        f"#fields {fields}",
    ]

    if trajectory.rotations is None:
        trajectory_data = np.c_[
            trajectory.timestamps, trajectory.path_lengths, trajectory.positions.xyz, trajectory.velocity_xyz
        ]
    else:
        trajectory_data = np.c_[
            trajectory.timestamps,
            trajectory.path_lengths,
            trajectory.positions.xyz,
            trajectory.rotations.as_quat(),
            trajectory.velocity_xyz,
        ]

    if trajectory.position_std is not None:
        trajectory_data = np.c_[trajectory_data, trajectory.position_std]

    output = io.StringIO()
    output.write("\n".join(header) + "\n")
    pd.DataFrame(trajectory_data).to_csv(output, header=False, index=False, float_format="%.9f")
    return output.getvalue()

def list_topics(filename: str | os.PathLike) -> dict[str, str]:
    """The topics of a bag with a supported message type, mapped to their message type.

    Args:
        filename (str): Path to the bag (file or ROS2 bag directory).

    Returns:
        dict[str, str]: Topic name to message type.

    See Also:
        [`trajectopy.io.trajectories_from_rosbag`][trajectopy.io.trajectories_from_rosbag]: reads the trajectories.

    Examples:
        >>> from trajectopy import io
        >>> io.list_topics("recording.mcap")["/odom"]
        'nav_msgs/msg/Odometry'
    """
    filename = os.fspath(filename)
    with AnyReader([Path(filename)], default_typestore=typestore) as reader:
        return {
            connection.topic: connection.msgtype
            for connection in reader.connections
            if connection.msgtype in ROS_MESSAGE_HANDLERS or connection.msgtype == PATH_MSGTYPE
        }

def trajectories_from_rosbag(filename: str | os.PathLike, *, topics: Iterable[str] | None = None) -> list[Trajectory]:
    """Creates trajectories from a ROS1 or ROS2 bag.

    Args:
        filename (str): Path to the bag: a ``.bag`` (ROS1), ``.mcap`` or ``.db3`` file, or a ROS2 bag directory.
        topics (Iterable[str] | None, optional): Topics to read. Defaults to all topics with a supported
            message type.

    Returns:
        list[Trajectory]: One trajectory per topic (and per frame pair of transform topics).

    See Also:
        [`trajectopy.io.list_topics`][trajectopy.io.list_topics]: lists the topics of a bag.

    Examples:
        >>> from trajectopy import io
        >>> trajectories = io.trajectories_from_rosbag("recording.mcap", topics=["/odom"])
        >>> [trajectory.name for trajectory in trajectories]
        ['/odom']
    """
    filename = os.fspath(filename)
    data = read_ros_bag(filename, topics=topics)

    trajectories = []
    for traj_key, traj_data in data.items():
        if not traj_data.get("x"):
            continue
        epsg = int(traj_data["epsg"][0]) if "epsg" in traj_data else 0
        pos = Positions(xyz=np.c_[traj_data["x"], traj_data["y"], traj_data["z"]], epsg=epsg)

        if any(len(traj_data.get(key, [])) != len(pos) for key in ["qx", "qy", "qz", "qw"]):
            rot = None
            logger.info("No rotation data found for trajectory %s", traj_key)
        else:
            rot = Rotation.from_quat(quat=np.c_[traj_data["qx"], traj_data["qy"], traj_data["qz"], traj_data["qw"]])

        position_std = None
        if all(len(traj_data.get(key, [])) == len(pos) for key in ["sx", "sy", "sz"]):
            position_std = np.c_[traj_data["sx"], traj_data["sy"], traj_data["sz"]]

        tstamps = np.array(traj_data.get("tstamps", np.arange(len(pos))), dtype=float)

        trajectories.append(
            Trajectory(name=traj_key, positions=pos, rotations=rot, timestamps=tstamps, position_std=position_std)
        )
        logger.info("Found trajectory: %s", traj_key)

    logger.info("Created %d trajectories from ROS bag %s", len(trajectories), filename)
    return trajectories

Reads an ATE result written by write_ate_result.

Files written by trajectopy versions with an earlier sign convention of the deviations are converted to the current one (test minus reference).

Parameters:

  • filename (str | PathLike) –

    Path of the file.

Returns:

  • ATEResult ( ATEResult ) –

    The result. Its alignment is None, since result files do not store it.

Examples:

>>> import trajectopy as tpy
>>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
>>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
>>> ate_result = tpy.ate(estimate, reference)
>>> from trajectopy import io
>>> io.write_ate_result(ate_result, "ate.result")
>>> io.read_ate_result("ate.result").alignment is None
True
Source code in trajectopy\io\results_io.py 
def read_ate_result(filename: str | os.PathLike) -> ATEResult:
    """Reads an ATE result written by [`write_ate_result`][trajectopy.io.write_ate_result].

    Files written by trajectopy versions with an earlier sign convention of the deviations are
    converted to the current one (test minus reference).

    Args:
        filename (str | os.PathLike): Path of the file.

    Returns:
        ATEResult: The result. Its ``alignment`` is None, since result files do not store it.

    Examples:
        >>> import trajectopy as tpy
        >>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
        >>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
        >>> ate_result = tpy.ate(estimate, reference)
        >>> from trajectopy import io
        >>> io.write_ate_result(ate_result, "ate.result")
        >>> io.read_ate_result("ate.result").alignment is None
        True
    """
    filename = os.fspath(filename)
    header_data = HeaderData.from_file(filename)
    deviation_data = pd.read_csv(filename, comment="#")
    sorting = Sorting(header_data.sorting)

    # the rows in the order the trajectory will have, so that the deviations stay with their poses: one pose
    # per timestamp and, if sorted by path length, ties in chronological order
    tstamps = deviation_data["time"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    chronological = np.argsort(tstamps, kind="stable")
    order = chronological[np.diff(tstamps[chronological], prepend=np.nan) != 0]
    if sorting == Sorting.PATH_LENGTH:
        path_lengths = deviation_data["arc_lengths"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        order = order[np.argsort(path_lengths[order], kind="stable")]
    deviation_data = deviation_data.iloc[order]

    tstamps = deviation_data["time"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    path_lengths = deviation_data["arc_lengths"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    positions = Positions(deviation_data[["pos_x", "pos_y", "pos_z"]].to_numpy(dtype=float), epsg=header_data.epsg)

    rot_columns = ["rot_x", "rot_y", "rot_z", "rot_w"]
    if all(column in deviation_data.columns for column in rot_columns):
        rotations = Rotation.from_quat(deviation_data[rot_columns].to_numpy(dtype=float))
    else:
        rotations = None

    pos_dev = deviation_data[["pos_dev_x", "pos_dev_y", "pos_dev_z"]].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    directed_pos_dev = deviation_data[["pos_dev_along", "pos_dev_cross_h", "pos_dev_cross_v"]].to_numpy(dtype=float)

    rot_dev_columns = ["rot_dev_x", "rot_dev_y", "rot_dev_z", "rot_dev_w"]
    if all(column in deviation_data.columns for column in rot_dev_columns):
        rot_dev = Rotation.from_quat(deviation_data[rot_dev_columns].to_numpy(dtype=float))
    else:
        rot_dev = None

    trajectory = Trajectory(
        name=header_data.name,
        positions=positions,
        rotations=rotations,
        timestamps=tstamps,
        path_lengths=path_lengths,
        sorting=sorting,
    )
    pos_dev, directed_pos_dev, rot_dev = convert_ate_deviations(
        header_data.deviations, pos_dev, directed_pos_dev, rot_dev
    )
    if directed_by := str(header_data.data.get("directed_by", "")):
        rotations_used = directed_by == "rotations"
    else:
        # earlier versions did not write it: rotations were used if either trajectory had some
        rotations_used = rot_dev is not None or rotations is not None
    abs_dev = AbsoluteTrajectoryDeviations(
        pos_dev=pos_dev, directed_pos_dev=directed_pos_dev, rot_dev=rot_dev, rotations_used=rotations_used
    )
    return ATEResult(trajectory=trajectory, abs_dev=abs_dev)

def write_ate_result(result: ATEResult, filename: str | os.PathLike, *, mode: str = "w") -> None:
    """Writes an ATE result as CSV file with a metadata header, which [`read_ate_result`][trajectopy.io.read_ate_result] and the GUI
    can read.

    The file contains the deviations of each pose together with the timestamps, path lengths and
    positions of the evaluated trajectory (see [`ATEResult.to_dataframe`][trajectopy.ATEResult.to_dataframe]).

    Args:
        result (ATEResult): Result to write.
        filename (str | os.PathLike): Path of the file.
        mode (str, optional): ``"w"`` (default) overwrites the file, ``"a"`` appends to it.

    See Also:
        [`trajectopy.ATEResult.to_file`][trajectopy.ATEResult.to_file]: the same as a method.

    Examples:
        >>> import trajectopy as tpy
        >>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
        >>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
        >>> ate_result = tpy.ate(estimate, reference)
        >>> from trajectopy import io
        >>> io.write_ate_result(ate_result, "ate.result")
        >>> len(io.read_ate_result("ate.result")) == len(ate_result)
        True
    """
    filename = os.fspath(filename)
    with open(filename, mode, newline="\n", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        file.write("#type ATE Result\n")  # so that the GUI recognizes the file
        file.write(f"#name {result.name}\n")
        file.write(f"#epsg {result.trajectory.positions.epsg}\n")
        file.write(f"#sorting {result.trajectory.sorting.value}\n")
        file.write(f"#deviations {DEVIATIONS_CONVENTION}\n")
        file.write(f"#directed_by {'rotations' if result.abs_dev.rotations_used else 'positions'}\n")
    result.to_dataframe().to_csv(filename, index=False, mode="a", float_format="%.12f")

>>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
>>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
>>> rpe_result = tpy.rpe(estimate, reference)

def read_rpe_result(filename: str | os.PathLike) -> RPEResult:
    """Reads an RPE result written by [`write_rpe_result`][trajectopy.io.write_rpe_result].

    Args:
        filename (str | os.PathLike): Path of the file.

    Returns:
        RPEResult: The result.

    Examples:
        >>> import trajectopy as tpy
        >>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
        >>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
        >>> rpe_result = tpy.rpe(estimate, reference)
        >>> from trajectopy import io
        >>> io.write_rpe_result(rpe_result, "rpe.result")
        >>> io.read_rpe_result("rpe.result").pos_drift_unit
        '%'
    """
    filename = os.fspath(filename)
    header_data = HeaderData.from_file(filename)
    deviation_data = pd.read_csv(filename, comment="#")

    pos_dev: dict[float, np.ndarray] = {}
    rot_dev: dict[float, np.ndarray] = {}
    pair_distance: dict[float, np.ndarray] = {}

    last_index = 0
    for index in header_data.num_pairs:
        dev_block = deviation_data.iloc[last_index : last_index + index, :]
        pair_distances = dev_block["pair_distance"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        pos_devs = dev_block["pos_dev"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        rot_devs = dev_block["rot_dev"].to_numpy(dtype=float) if "rot_dev" in deviation_data.columns else np.array([])

        mean_dist = float(np.mean(pair_distances))
        pair_distance[mean_dist] = pair_distances
        pos_dev[mean_dist] = pos_devs
        rot_dev[mean_dist] = rot_devs

        last_index += index

    rpe_dev = RelativeTrajectoryDeviations(
        pair_distance=pair_distance,
        pos_dev=pos_dev,
        rot_dev=rot_dev,
        pair_distance_unit=header_data.relative_dist_unit,
    )

    return RPEResult(rpe_dev=rpe_dev, name=header_data.name)

def write_alignment_result(result: AlignmentResult, filename: str | os.PathLike, *, mode: str = "w") -> None:
    """Writes an alignment result to a file that [`read_alignment_result`][trajectopy.io.read_alignment_result] and the GUI can read.

    Args:
        result (AlignmentResult): Result to write.
        filename (str | os.PathLike): Path of the file.
        mode (str, optional): ``"w"`` (default) overwrites the file, ``"a"`` appends to it.

    See Also:
        [`trajectopy.AlignmentResult.to_file`][trajectopy.AlignmentResult.to_file]: the same as a method.

    Examples:
        >>> import trajectopy as tpy
        >>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
        >>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
        >>> alignment = tpy.estimate_alignment(estimate, reference)
        >>> from trajectopy import io
        >>> io.write_alignment_result(alignment, "alignment.result")
        >>> io.read_alignment_result("alignment.result") == alignment
        True
    """
    filename = os.fspath(filename)
    with open(filename, mode, newline="\n", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        file.write("#type Alignment\n")  # so that the GUI recognizes the file
        file.write(f"#name {result.name}\n")
        if not result.converged:  # files without this line hold converged results
            file.write("#converged false\n")

    result.position_parameters.to_dataframe().to_csv(
        filename, header=False, index=False, mode="a", float_format="%.17g"
    )
    write_sensor_rotation_parameters(result.rotation_parameters, filename)

def read_alignment_parameters(filename: str | os.PathLike) -> AlignmentParameters:
    """Reads alignment parameters written by [`write_alignment_parameters`][trajectopy.io.write_alignment_parameters].

    Args:
        filename (str | os.PathLike): Path of the file.

    Returns:
        AlignmentParameters: The parameter values, which of them are enabled and, if the file contains it,
        their covariance matrix.

    Examples:
        >>> import trajectopy as tpy
        >>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
        >>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
        >>> alignment = tpy.estimate_alignment(estimate, reference)
        >>> from trajectopy import io
        >>> io.write_alignment_parameters(alignment.position_parameters, "parameters.csv")
        >>> parameters = io.read_alignment_parameters("parameters.csv")
        >>> parameters.num_enabled
        6
    """
    filename = os.fspath(filename)
    alignment_data = pd.read_csv(filename, comment="#", header=None)
    params = AlignmentParameters()
    params.values = alignment_data.iloc[:11, 0].to_numpy()
    params.enabled_bool_list = [str(item).lower() != "false" for item in alignment_data.iloc[:11, 1].to_list()]

    if alignment_data.shape[1] > 2:
        params.set_covariance_matrix(alignment_data.iloc[:11, 2:].to_numpy())

    return params

def read_sensor_rotation_parameters(filename: str | os.PathLike) -> SensorRotationParameters:
    """Reads the sensor rotation parameters of an alignment result file.

    The sensor rotation follows the eleven alignment parameters, so that the file has 14 data lines.

    Args:
        filename (str | os.PathLike): Path of an alignment result file.

    Returns:
        SensorRotationParameters: The rotation angles (radians) and which of them are enabled.

    Raises:
        TrajectopyIOError: If the file does not contain exactly 14 data lines.

    Examples:
        >>> import trajectopy as tpy
        >>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
        >>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
        >>> alignment = tpy.estimate_alignment(estimate, reference)
        >>> from trajectopy import io
        >>> io.write_alignment_result(alignment, "alignment.result")
        >>> io.read_sensor_rotation_parameters("alignment.result").num_enabled
        0
    """
    filename = os.fspath(filename)
    alignment_data = pd.read_csv(filename, comment="#", header=None)

    if len(alignment_data) != 14:
        raise TrajectopyIOError("Alignment file with sensor rotation information must contain 14 lines!")

    params = SensorRotationParameters()
    params.values = alignment_data.iloc[11:, 0].to_numpy()
    params.enabled_bool_list = [str(item).lower() != "false" for item in alignment_data.iloc[11:, 1].to_list()]
    return params

write_kml(
    trajectory: Trajectory,
    filename: str | PathLike,
    *,
    color: str = DEFAULT_KML_COLOR,
    field: str | None = None,
    colormap: str = "rdylbu",
    max_std: float = 3.0,
    value_range: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    color_classes: int = DEFAULT_COLOR_CLASSES,
    heights: str = "ground",
    height_offset: float = 0.0,
    extrude: bool = False,
    line_width: float = 3.0,
    precision: float = 1e-06,
) -> None

Exports a trajectory to a Google Earth KML file.

The trajectory is written as a time-stamped track (gx:Track): Google Earth shows its path and plays it back with the time slider. Optionally, it is colored by a field (speed, height or time).

Requires the trajectory to have a valid EPSG code so it can be converted to WGS84 (EPSG:4326).

Parameters:

  • trajectory (Trajectory) –

    Trajectory to export.

  • filename (str) –

    The output filename (e.g., "track.kml").

  • color (str, default: DEFAULT_KML_COLOR ) –

    Color of the track and its points as "#RRGGBB" or "#RRGGBBAA", if it is not colored by a field. Defaults to red.

  • field (str, default: None ) –

    Key of the field that colors the line: "speed", "height" or "time". Defaults to none (one color).

  • colormap (str, default: 'rdylbu' ) –

    Color scale of the field: "rdylbu" (blue = low, red = high, like the plots) or "viridis" (colorblind-safe). Defaults to "rdylbu".

  • max_std (float, default: 3.0 ) –

    The color scale is clipped to mean ± max_std standard deviations (0 = minimum to maximum). Ignored if value_range is given. Defaults to 3.0, like the plots.

  • value_range (tuple[float, float], default: None ) –

    Fixed (lower, upper) limits of the color scale, e.g. to compare several exports; values beyond them get the color of the nearest limit. Defaults to none.

  • color_classes (int, default: DEFAULT_COLOR_CLASSES ) –

    Number of colors of the scale. Defaults to 11.

  • heights (str, default: 'ground' ) –

    Vertical placement: "ground" (clamped to the terrain), "ellipsoidal" (the trajectory's heights are ellipsoidal heights, e.g. GNSS; converted with the EGM96 geoid, which needs an internet connection the first time) or "sea_level" (the heights are above sea level). Defaults to "ground".

  • height_offset (float, default: 0.0 ) –

    Meters added to the heights; with "ground", the trajectory floats this far above the terrain. Defaults to 0.

  • extrude (bool, default: False ) –

    Connect the trajectory to the ground with a vertical curtain (not with "ground" and no offset). Defaults to False.

  • line_width (float, default: 3.0 ) –

    Line width in pixels. Defaults to 3.

  • precision (float, default: 1e-06 ) –

    Coordinate precision in degrees. Defaults to 1e-6 (about 0.1 m).

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    If the trajectory does not have a known EPSG code, an option is invalid, or the geoid model is not available.

See Also

trajectopy.Trajectory.to_kml: the same as a method.

Examples:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import trajectopy as tpy
>>> from trajectopy import io
>>> xyz = np.column_stack([364000.0 + np.arange(10.0), np.full(10, 5621000.0), np.full(10, 60.0)])
>>> track = tpy.Trajectory(tpy.Positions(xyz, epsg=25832), timestamps=np.arange(10.0))
>>> io.write_kml(track, "track.kml", color="#1f77b4")
