def figure_widget(self, index: int) -> _FigureWidget | None:
    """Returns the widget of a tab, or None if the tab has not been opened (rendered) yet.

    Args:
        index (int): Index of the tab.

    Returns:
        QtWidgets.QWidget | None: The widget of the figure.
    """
    container = self.tabs.widget(index)
    if container is None or (layout := container.layout()) is None or layout.count() == 0:
        return None
    widget = layout.itemAt(0).widget()  # type: ignore[union-attr]
    return widget if isinstance(widget, _FigureWidget) else None

def export_current(self) -> None:
    """Asks for a file and exports the figure (and variant) of the current tab."""
    index = self.tabs.currentIndex()
    if index < 0:
        return
    figure = self.figures[index]
    widget = self.figure_widget(index)
    variant = widget.current_variant if widget is not None else None
    stem = _safe_filename(f"{figure.title} {variant}" if variant else figure.title)
    path, _ = QtWidgets.QFileDialog.getSaveFileName(
        self,
        "Export Plot",
        f"{stem}.{self.export_format}",
        "Images (*.png *.jpg *.svg)",
        options=_dialog_options(),
    )
    if not path:
        return
    if not os.path.splitext(path)[1]:
        path += f".{self.export_format}"  # the image format follows from the extension
    self._report_failure(lambda: figure.export(path, variant=variant, width=self.export_width))

def export_figures(
    figures: Sequence[Figure], directory: str | os.PathLike, *, export_format: str = "png", width: int = 1600
) -> list[str]:
    """Exports all figures (and all their variants) to image files in ``directory``.

    The files are named after the position, title and variant of the figures, e.g.
    ``01_ATE_Position.png``.

    Args:
        figures (Sequence[Figure]): Figures to export.
        directory (str | os.PathLike): Folder of the files; it is created if needed.
        export_format (str, optional): ``png``, ``jpg`` or ``svg``. Defaults to "png".
        width (int, optional): Width of raster images in pixels. Defaults to 1600.

    Returns:
        list[str]: Paths of the written files.

    See Also:
        [`trajectopy.visualization.show`][trajectopy.visualization.show]: shows figures in a window instead.

    Examples:
        >>> import trajectopy as tpy
        >>> reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
        >>> estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")
        >>> ate_result = tpy.ate(estimate, reference)
        >>> from trajectopy import visualization as vis
        >>> paths = vis.export_figures([vis.ate_figure([ate_result])], "plots", width=800)
        >>> import os
        >>> [os.path.basename(path) for path in paths]
        ['01_ATE.png']
    """
    os.makedirs(directory, exist_ok=True)
    paths = []
    for index, figure in enumerate(figures, start=1):
        for variant in figure.variants:
            stem = _safe_filename(f"{index:02d}_{figure.title}" + (f"_{variant}" if variant else ""))
            path = os.path.join(directory, f"{stem}.{export_format}")
            figure.export(path, variant=variant, width=width)
            paths.append(path)
    return paths

def set_theme(*, dark: bool) -> None:

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
The user guide explains the concepts of trajectopy and shows how to use them, from loading trajectories to reports of several evaluated estimates. New to trajectopy? Start with the Getting Started tutorial. The API reference describes every class and function in detail.

Topic Contents Trajectories Creating, loading, saving, selecting and transforming trajectories; coordinate systems Alignment Estimating and applying the transformation between two trajectories Evaluation Absolute trajectory error (ATE), relative pose error (RPE), statistics, reports Visualization Interactive plots and image export Google Earth Export of trajectories and ATE results as KML File Formats Trajectory files, ROS bags and the files trajectopy writes Settings All processing and plot settings GUI The graphical user interface Command Line Evaluation, alignment and conversion from the shell Glossary The terms used in trajectopy

The examples use the files in the example_data folder of the repository: the ground truth of a KITTI sequence and the estimates of two visual SLAM systems, ORB-SLAM and S-PTAM.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Trajectopy is imported as tpy; the plotting module as vis:

import trajectopy as tpy
from trajectopy import visualization as vis

The public API consists of the names in the namespaces trajectopy, trajectopy.io, trajectopy.visualization and trajectopy.exceptions. Import from these namespaces, not from the modules the names are defined in; the API policy describes which changes to expect between versions.

All functions follow the same conventions:

  • Trajectory and reference: functions that compare two trajectories take the trajectory to evaluate (or to align) first and the reference second; the parameters are called trajectory and other.
  • Inputs are not modified: functions and methods that change a trajectory return a new one. Pass inplace=True to change the given trajectory instead. Always use the return value: trajectory = tpy.align(trajectory, reference). Exceptions are the methods Trajectory.set_sorting, ATEResult.set_sorting and ATEResult.remove_ate_above, which change the object itself.
  • One settings argument: processing functions with settings take a settings argument, either their own settings type (e.g. MatchingSettings) or the complete ProcessingSettings, of which they use the part they need (ate, which needs several parts, takes only ProcessingSettings). None means the default settings.
  • Options are keyword arguments: only the data (trajectories, results, file names, indices) and the settings are positional arguments; all options are passed by name, e.g. tpy.interpolate(trajectory, index, method="linear").
  • Options as strings: options such as the matching method are enumerations, but strings are accepted as well (in any case), e.g. tpy.MatchingSettings(method="nearest_temporal").
  • Units: positions, path lengths and position deviations are in meters, timestamps in seconds, angles in radians, unless stated otherwise.
  • Deviations: deviations are always evaluated trajectory minus reference.
  • Files: functions that read or write files accept strings and pathlib.Path objects. Writers overwrite existing files; those with a mode argument append to them with mode="a". Only write_sensor_rotation_parameters and SensorRotationParameters.to_file always append (to an alignment result file).

docs.title: Alignment
docs.text: Two trajectories can only be compared pose by pose if they are given in the same coordinate frame and with the same time reference. A SLAM estimate, for example, starts in a frame of its own, and the clock of a sensor may be offset from that of the reference. The alignment estimates the transformation between both trajectories.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
The alignment estimates up to 11 parameters with a least squares adjustment of matched poses (see the paper for the model):

Parameters Meaning Estimated by default Translation x, y, z Shift between the frames [m] yes Rotation x, y, z Rotation between the frames [rad] yes Scale Scale factor, e.g. for monocular visual odometry no Time shift Offset between the clocks [s] no Leverarm x, y, z Offset between the reference points of both platforms, in the body frame [m]; needs orientations no

Additionally, a constant sensor rotation (mounting rotation between the body frames) can be computed from the orientations after the least squares adjustment.

Which parameters are estimated is set in the alignment settings; the settings also contain the standard deviations that weight the observations and a preprocessing step that selects the poses to use. The leverarm needs the orientations of the trajectory to align; estimating it without them raises AlignmentError.

The time shift is the offset of the clock of the aligned trajectory: apply_alignment subtracts it from its timestamps. A positive time shift means that the timestamps of the trajectory are too large, e.g. a time shift of 0.1 s means that the pose stamped 10.1 s was taken when the reference shows 10.0 s.

docs.title: Estimating and Applying an Alignment
docs.text:
import trajectopy as tpy

reference = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_gt.traj")
estimate = tpy.Trajectory.from_file("./example_data/KITTI_ORB.traj")

alignment = tpy.estimate_alignment(estimate, reference)
print(alignment)
print(alignment.position_parameters)

aligned = tpy.apply_alignment(estimate, alignment)

estimate_alignment matches the poses of both trajectories (see Matching), estimates the parameters and returns an AlignmentResult. apply_alignment applies it to a trajectory, not necessarily the one it was estimated for, e.g. to all trajectories recorded with the same sensor setup. align does both in one step:

aligned = tpy.align(estimate, reference)

Both functions take AlignmentSettings or the complete ProcessingSettings; only the latter also sets the matching (with AlignmentSettings, the default matching settings are used).

An ATE evaluation aligns the trajectories itself and keeps the alignment in its result (ate_result.alignment).

docs.title: Choosing the Parameters
docs.text:
settings = tpy.AlignmentSettings()
settings.estimation_settings.scale = True  # monocular visual odometry has no metric scale
settings.estimation_settings.time_shift = True

alignment = tpy.estimate_alignment(estimate, reference, settings)

AlignmentEstimationSettings.from_components enables groups of parameters at once; similarity enables the translation, the rotation and the scale:

settings.estimation_settings = tpy.AlignmentEstimationSettings.from_components(
    similarity=True, time_shift=True, leverarm=False
)

docs.title: Inspecting the Result
docs.text:
The estimated parameters are AlignmentParameters: each parameter has a value and a variance, and the parameters share a covariance matrix.

parameters = alignment.position_parameters
print(parameters.sim_trans_x.value, parameters.sim_trans_x.variance)
print(parameters.time_shift.value)
print(parameters.sim3_matrix)  # 4x4 similarity transformation
print(alignment.converged)  # False if the least squares adjustment did not converge

If the adjustment does not converge, the parameters keep their initial values.

trajectopy.visualization.alignment_figures plots the covariance and correlation matrices, which show whether parameters could be told apart with the data at hand (see Visualization).

Alignments are saved and loaded with to_file and AlignmentResult.from_file.

docs.title: Initial Values
docs.text:
initial_parameters starts the adjustment at given values instead of an approximate solution of its own, e.g. from the interactive alignment in the GUI. Parameters that are not estimated keep these values. A large time offset (e.g. between unrelated clocks) can be given this way; then only the remaining offset is estimated:

prior = tpy.AlignmentParameters()
prior.time_shift.value = 0.0  # e.g. a known offset between the clocks in seconds
alignment = tpy.estimate_alignment(estimate, reference, initial_parameters=prior)

docs.title: Simpler Alignments
docs.text:
adopt_first_pose shifts a trajectory so that its first position coincides with the first position of the reference, and rotates its orientations so that its first orientation coincides with the first orientation of the reference. The positions are only shifted, not rotated. Both trajectories should be matched first, so that their first poses correspond.

matched, matched_reference = tpy.match_trajectories(estimate, reference)
first_pose_aligned = tpy.adopt_first_pose(matched, matched_reference)

docs.title: Matching
docs.text:
Alignment and ATE compare corresponding poses. match_trajectories finds them with the method of the matching settings and returns copies of both trajectories that contain only the matched poses, in the same order:

Method Matching interpolation (default) The trajectory is interpolated at the timestamps of the reference nearest_temporal Pose with the nearest timestamp, within max_time_diff nearest_spatial Nearest position, within max_distance; needs no common time reference nearest_spatial_interpolated Projection onto a line through the k_nearest nearest reference positions 
matched, matched_reference = tpy.match_trajectories(
    estimate, reference, tpy.MatchingSettings(method="nearest_temporal")
)
print(len(matched) == len(matched_reference))

If the time spans of both trajectories do not overlap at all, the interpolation and nearest_temporal methods first estimate the time offset roughly by matching the positions. Clocks that are offset but still overlap are not detected; estimate the time shift with the alignment, or give it as initial value.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text: The trajectopy command starts the GUI. With a subcommand, it evaluates, aligns and converts trajectories without a GUI, e.g. in scripts, on servers or in CI pipelines. trajectopy <command> --help lists the options of a command.

docs.title: Starting the GUI
docs.text:
trajectopy [-h] [--version] [--single-thread] [--plot-settings PLOT_SETTINGS] [files ...]
Argument Description files Project (.tpy), trajectory (.traj, .bag, .mcap, …) or result (.result) files to open at start. Trajectories and results are added to the project; of several projects, only the first is opened. Bag directories cannot be opened this way. --version, -v Show the version and exit. --single-thread Process in the GUI thread instead of a background thread, e.g. for debugging. The GUI does not respond while processing. On by default when trajectopy runs under a debugger. --plot-settings PLOT_SETTINGS JSON file with plot settings; settings missing in the file keep their default values. If the file cannot be read, the GUI logs the error and starts with the default plot settings. -h, --help Show the help and exit. 
trajectopy ground_truth.traj slam.traj
trajectopy flight.tpy
trajectopy --plot-settings plot_settings.json

A project contains its own plot settings, which replace those given with --plot-settings when it is opened. The Windows app has no console, so it prints nothing: neither --version and --help nor the output of the commands below; the version is shown in Help → About. The apps for macOS and Linux print to the terminal they are started from (on macOS, start the program Trajectopy.app/Contents/MacOS/Trajectopy). For scripts and pipelines, the Python package is the better choice.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Description ate Absolute trajectory error of one or more trajectories against a reference rpe Relative pose error (drift) of one or more trajectories against a reference evaluate ATE and RPE of one or more trajectories against a reference align Align trajectories to a reference and print the parameters convert Convert trajectories between formats (and coordinate systems) info Show a summary of trajectory files and the topics of ROS bags

All commands read trajectopy, TUM, KITTI and EuRoC files and ROS bags (.bag, .mcap, .db3 or a bag directory). A reference bag with several supported topics needs --ref-topic. Errors are printed as one line and reported with exit code 1 (2 for invalid arguments or input, e.g. a missing file), so the commands can be used in pipelines; with --verbose, errors with exit code 1 show their full traceback instead.

Output files named after a trajectory or result (<name> below) replace every character other than letters, digits, -, _ and . with _, e.g. KITTI ORB vs. KITTI Ground Truth becomes KITTI_ORB_vs._KITTI_Ground_Truth.

# ATE of two estimates; prints a summary table
trajectopy ate orb.traj sptam.traj --ref gt.traj

# ATE and RPE with custom settings: summary table, result files, figures and an HTML report
trajectopy evaluate orb.traj sptam.traj --ref gt.traj --settings settings.json \
    --table summary.md --output-dir results --figures figures --report report.html

# RPE of an odometry topic of a ROS2 bag against a TUM file
trajectopy rpe recording.mcap --topic /odom --ref gt.tum

# Align a trajectory and save it together with the alignment parameters
trajectopy align estimate.traj --ref gt.traj -o aligned.traj --parameters alignment.result

# Convert between formats and coordinate systems
trajectopy convert poses.txt --format kitti --to tum -o poses.tum
trajectopy convert gnss.traj --epsg 25832 -o gnss_utm.traj

# Show the trajectories of a file and the topics of a bag
trajectopy info recording.bag

docs.title: Options of All Commands
docs.text: Option Description files Trajectory files or ROS bags --topic TOPIC Topic to read from ROS bags (repeatable); all supported topics by default --format FORMAT Format of the trajectory files: auto (default), trajectopy, tum, kitti or euroc --quiet, -q Print only warnings and errors --verbose Print debug messages and the traceback of errors (except invalid input)

docs.title: ate, rpe and evaluate
docs.text:
Option Description --ref, -r REF Reference (ground truth) trajectory file or ROS bag (required) --ref-topic TOPIC Topic of the reference in a ROS bag --ref-format FORMAT Format of the reference file --settings, -s FILE JSON file with processing settings --no-align Evaluate without estimating an alignment first --table, -t FILE Write the summary table to this file --table-format FORMAT csv, markdown or latex; by default derived from the extension of --table (.md, .tex, otherwise CSV) --no-ci Leave out the confidence intervals (faster) --output-dir, -o DIR Write the result files (.result) to this directory --figures DIR Export all figures to this directory (requires trajectopy[plot]) --plot-settings FILE JSON plot settings for figures and the report --report FILE Write a self-contained HTML report to this file --no-report-figures Leave the figures out of the report

--output-dir and --figures are created if they do not exist. --output-dir receives <name>_ate.result and <name>_rpe.result for each trajectory, where <name> is the name of the result (<trajectory> vs. <reference>), and for each ATE result (unless --no-align is given) its alignment as <name>_alignment.result. Existing files are overwritten.

Unless --no-align is given, rpe and evaluate compute the RPE of the aligned trajectory, with the alignment of the settings. The RPE of trajectopy.rpe in Python and of the GUI uses the trajectory as it is. Both agree for the default rigid body alignment, which does not change relative poses; with scale, time shift, lever arm or sensor rotation, they differ. --quiet also suppresses the summary table, which is not printed either when it is written with --table.

With a directory as --output, the aligned trajectories are written as <name>_aligned.traj (.tum, .kitti or .csv with --to tum, kitti or euroc), where <name> is the name of the trajectory. Several trajectories need an existing directory as --output; --parameters then holds the alignment of the last one.
